images.filename: 1 Sri Kesgarh Takhat Anandpur Sahib Khalsa birthplace Punjab India.jpg
images.caption:
Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib also known as Anandpur Sahib is the historic site in Sikhism where Khalsa was founded by Guru Gobind Singh.
It is located near Himalayan foothills near the river Satluj. The site is second only to Amritsar, the city of Golden Temple in the Sikh tradition.
Anandpur Sahib was founded in the year 1665 by the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur.

A small town is the site of major annual gathering of Sikhs for Hola Mohalla festival every year in spring when other parts of India are celebrating Holi. It is a festive gathering with a display of martial arts, fairs and gaiety.

images.caption:
Kavi Kuvresh on meeting Guru Gobind Singh: 
“We Hindus lack the strength to withstand the might of the Turks. We fear that our religion and common culture will be destroyed and that we will be forced to convert to Islam.  I left the Mughal emperor’s Darbar because of this terrible fear and came to You hoping to save my religion.” 
The forced conversions to Islam under emperor Aurangzeb
Why did more than 100 poets across religious boundaries flock to Anandpur Sahib during the rule of Guru Gobind Singh ji ? This is a topic that has aroused the interest of many scholars over the centuries. While most poets came due to the Guru’s extensive patronage and appreciation of the arts, in some cases, persecution and fleeing forced conversions to Islam was the reason. This was the case with many poets, amongst these the most famous Bhai Nand Lal Goyā and Kavi Kuvresh.
The topic of Mughal persecution is noted in many of the Anandpuri writings. The Hindu court poet Kuvresh who had worked for the Mughal Darbar stated “it was Emperor Aurangzeb’s intention to convert us all to Islam” while the poet Ani Rai wrote that “Hindus were converted into Muslims and temples were daily razed to the ground” (translated by Professor Louis Fenech).
The fanatical emperor Aurangzeb was keen on converting the Hindu populace to Islam in order to turn the Mughal empire into a Muslim majority state. In the fortified city of Anandpur Sahib, many Hindu poets from the Mughal Darbar found safety and an opportunity to continue practising their artistic skills.
For this reason, Kavi Kuvresh pays eternal, poetic homage to the Guru who saved so many of his fellow Hindu poets fleeing persecution:
ਗੁਰ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਨਰਿੰਦ ਹੈ ਤੇਗ ਬਹਾਦੁਰ ਨੰਦ
ਜਿਨ ਤੇ ਜੀਵਤ ਹੈਂ ਸਕਲ ਭੂਤਲ ਕਵਿ ਬੁਧਿ ਬ੍ਰਿੰਦ

Guru Gobind is the (true) King of All and the son of Tegh Bahadur (who likewise protected Hindus who were threatened to convert). It is only because of Him, that the entire community of poets and intellectuals still survive and thrive in this world!

images.filename: Select Overview of Literature and Scriptures Studied in the Anandpur Darbar.jpg
images.caption:
A selection of literature in the Anandpur Library
For a quarter of a century (1679-1704) the city of Anandpur was a cultural hub and advanced centre of learning. More than a hundred Sikh, Hindu and Muslim scholars and intellectuals headed for the city from across the Indo-Islamic world in their pursuit for a liberal patron who would sponsor their literary endeavors.
They found this liberal patron in the person of Guru Gobind Singh, who was busy setting up a massive library in Anandpur, that also included a large manuscript collection of his own, as most likely testified in a later manuscript copy of a book on falconry and hunting:
ਅਥ ਬਾਜ਼ਨਾਮਾ ਨਕਲ ਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਪੋਥੀ ਕਾ ਲਿਖਿਆ।
Now begins the Bāznāmā. It has been copied from the Guru’s own manuscript.
Several early traditions narrate how the Guru sent Sikhs across the Indian subcontinent to invite scholars to Anandpur. Other Sikhs were sent out across the subcontinent to locate books containing valuable knowledge that could be sent to Anandpur to enrich its expanding library collection.

More than a hundred such scholars arrived. Collectively these scholars and poets of all faiths translated the classics of the ancient Sanskrit and Persian civilisations. The extant manuscript record show a magnitude of topics explored by the scholars and Sikhs in this period, ranging from ancient philosophy, history, politics and governance, zoology, manuals on how to write beautiful poetry and literature, dictionaries and lexica, eroticism, fables for kids and youth, architecture, geography, mysticism, political satire, love poetry etc. There were no taboos and all topics seem to have been explored in the Anandpur court.
